standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.6, the sentence 'In the case where we have a discrete and finite number of values for $\mathbf{X}_i$, the IPW estimator is logically equivalent to the plug-in estimator from Section 7.2.1', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 266 (PDF p. 284), paragraph after Definition 7.2.6. Section 7.2.1 plug-in estimator: p. 256 (PDF p. 274). Section 7.2.5: p. 264 (PDF p. 282)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] In the case where we have a discrete and finite number of values for $\mathbf{X}_i$, the IPW estimator is logically equivalent to the plug-in estimator from Section 7.2.1 (Plug-In Estimation). [What is refuted] Equality of $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[\tau_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{Y_iD_i}{\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)} - \frac{Y_i(1 - D_i)}{1 - \hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right)$ (Definition 7.2.6) and the post-stratification plug-in estimator of Section 7.2.1 whenever $\mathbf{X}_i$ has finitely many values, with $\hat p_D$ the ML plug-in estimate from a binary choice model that Section 7.2.5 adopts. Equality when each fitted propensity is the observed treated fraction in its cell is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Eighteen units with $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, Z_i)$, six in each cell $Z_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$. Cell $Z = -1$: three treated units, each with $Y_i = 4$, and three control units, each with $Y_i = 3$. Cell $Z = 0$: one treated unit with $Y_i = 3$ and five control units, each with $Y_i = 2$. Cell $Z = 1$: five treated units, each with $Y_i = 4$, and one control unit with $Y_i = 3$. Then: (a) the logit model $p_{\alpha, \beta}(z) = \frac{e^{\alpha + \beta z}}{1 + e^{\alpha + \beta z}}$ has the unique ML estimate $(\hat\alpha, \hat\beta) = (0, \log 2)$, with fitted probabilities $(\hat p_D(-1), \hat p_D(0), \hat p_D(1)) = (\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{3})$ (the score equations hold: $3 - 6 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1$, $1 - 6 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = -2$, $5 - 6 \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 1$, with $1 - 2 + 1 = 0$ and $-1 + 0 + 1 = 0$); the observed treated fractions are $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{5}{6})$; (b) the plug-in estimator of Section 7.2.1 is $\frac{6}{18}(4 - 3) + \frac{6}{18}(3 - 2) + \frac{6}{18}(4 - 3) = 1$; (c) the IPW estimator is $\frac{1}{18}\left[\left(\frac{3 \cdot 4}{1/3} - \frac{3 \cdot 3}{2/3}\right) + \left(\frac{1 \cdot 3}{1/2} - \frac{5 \cdot 2}{1/2}\right) + \left(\frac{5 \cdot 4}{2/3} - \frac{1 \cdot 3}{1/3}\right)\right] = \frac{1}{18}\left[\frac{45}{2} - 14 + 21\right] = \frac{59}{36}$; (d) $\frac{59}{36} - 1 = \frac{23}{36} \ne 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Section 7.2.1, p. 256 (PDF p. 274)] the plug-in estimator is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau_i] = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]}\left(\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] - \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 0, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]\right)\widehat{\Pr}[\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]}\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_iD_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i(1 - D_i) \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - D_i) \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}\right) \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{n}$, where $\mathrm{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $\widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is the set of all observed values of $\mathbf{X}_i$. [Footnote 12] This requires that we have at least one treated unit and one control unit with $\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}$ for every covariate profile $\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, otherwise we will have a zero in the denominator. [Definition 7.2.6, p. 266] Given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, the inverse probability–weighted estimator for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[\tau_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{Y_iD_i}{\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)} - \frac{Y_i(1 - D_i)}{1 - \hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right)$. [Section 7.2.5, p. 264] $\hat p_D(\mathbf{x}) = h(\mathbf{x}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{ML})$; 'Regardless of the exact specification, we will assume as we proceed that we are using an ML plug-in estimate from a binary choice model'.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor: the parallel of P001-C06-E004 for causal inference. The validator proves that the ML fit is the unique global maximizer (strict concavity; Hessian $\mathrm{diag}(-\frac{25}{6}, -\frac{8}{3})$ at the fit) and that the sample has positive probability under an i.i.d. population with a correctly specified logit propensity and strong ignorability. The observed treated fractions give IPW the value 1, equal to the plug-in estimator.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.6, equivalence of the IPW estimator and the post-stratification plug-in estimator of the ATE, corrected: it holds when each fitted propensity equals the observed treated fraction in its covariate cell
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] With discrete covariates taking finitely many values, the IPW estimator equals the post-stratification plug-in estimator in Section 7.2.1 when each fitted propensity equals the observed treated fraction in its covariate cell (as under saturated propensity estimation), provided both treatment arms are represented in every observed cell. [In full] Let $(Y_i, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ be a sample with $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$, let $\mathcal{C}$ be the finite set of observed values of $\mathbf{X}_i$, and for $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$ let $N_{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$, $N_{1\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i D_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$, $N_{0\mathbf{x}} = N_{\mathbf{x}} - N_{1\mathbf{x}}$, with $N_{1\mathbf{x}} > 0$ and $N_{0\mathbf{x}} > 0$, and let $S_{1\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i Y_iD_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$, $S_{0\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i Y_i(1 - D_i)\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$. Let $q_{\mathbf{x}} = \hat p_D(\mathbf{x}) \in (0, 1)$. Then (i) $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[\tau_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}}\left(\frac{S_{1\mathbf{x}}}{q_{\mathbf{x}}} - \frac{S_{0\mathbf{x}}}{1 - q_{\mathbf{x}}}\right)$ and the plug-in estimator of Section 7.2.1 equals $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}} N_{\mathbf{x}}\left(\frac{S_{1\mathbf{x}}}{N_{1\mathbf{x}}} - \frac{S_{0\mathbf{x}}}{N_{0\mathbf{x}}}\right)$; (ii) if $q_{\mathbf{x}} = N_{1\mathbf{x}}/N_{\mathbf{x}}$ for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$, the two estimators are equal; (iii) for fixed covariates, treatments and fitted probabilities, the two estimators are equal for all outcome vectors if and only if $q_{\mathbf{x}} = N_{1\mathbf{x}}/N_{\mathbf{x}}$ for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$.

[Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph after Definition 7.2.7 (Stabilized IPW Estimator for Causal Inference): the two sums whose between-sample variation the stabilized estimator accounts for, corrected (the treatment-arm indicators)
canonical_claim.location: p. 267 (PDF p. 285), Definition 7.2.7 and the paragraph after it
canonical_claim.statement: [Definition 7.2.7, as printed; unchanged] Stabilized IPW Estimator for Causal Inference. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, the stabilized IPW estimator for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{SIPW}[\tau_i] = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_iD_i}{\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{D_i}{\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}} - \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_i(1 - D_i)}{1 - \hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - D_i}{1 - \hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}}$. [Printed passage] When $\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$ converges (in an appropriate functional sense) to $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$, then the denominator of each fraction will converge in probability to one. To see this, note that, with the true propensity score, $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{D_i}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - D_i}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = 1$. ... Because the stabilized IPW estimator accounts for this between-sample variation in $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}$, it typically confers efficiency gains over the IPW estimator in practice. [Corrected sums] ... this between-sample variation in $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{D_i}{\hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - D_i}{1 - \hat p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ ... (with $p_D$ in place of $\hat p_D$ in an explanation that uses the true scores). [Formal content] Let $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$ and $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. Then $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{D_i}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right] = 1$ and $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - D_i}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right] = 1$, so for i.i.d. units $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{D_i}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - D_i}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = 1$ for every $n$; whereas $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] > 1$ and $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] > 1$, so the all-unit sums printed in the passage are not the denominators of Definition 7.2.7.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.3.1, the sentence 'the estimand $\mathrm{E}[p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)\tau_i]$ ... is equivalent to the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1]$', as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] We might also choose an estimand that weights members of the population by some function of the propensity score. For example, the estimand $\mathrm{E}[p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)\tau_i]$, which weights by the propensity score itself, is equivalent to the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1]$. The ATT is nonparametrically identified under the CIA and a weaker positivity assumption, $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < \epsilon < 1$. [What is refuted] The equality $\mathrm{E}[p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1]$ under the conditional independence assumption. The normalized statement is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $\mathbf{X}_i = 0$ (constant), $Y_i(0) = 0$ and $Y_i(1) = 1$ for every unit, so $\tau_i = 1$, and let $\Pr[D_i = 1] = \frac{1}{4}$ (two atoms: $D_i = 0$ with probability $\frac{3}{4}$, $D_i = 1$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$). The potential outcomes are constant, so $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$; $p_D(0) = \frac{1}{4}$, so positivity holds (with $\epsilon = \frac{1}{8}$), and the ATT paragraph's bound $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < \epsilon < 1$ holds with $\epsilon = \frac{3}{8}$. canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] For example, the estimand $\frac{\mathrm{E}[p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)]}$, which weights by the propensity score itself, is equivalent to the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1]$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Glossary of Mathematical Notation, the row for set subtraction ($\backslash$): the relative-complement identity, corrected ($A\backslash B = A \cap B^C$)
canonical_claim.location: p. 283 (PDF p. 301), row '$\backslash$' (Set subtraction); the rows for $A^C$, $\cup$ and $\cap$ on the same page
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement] Set subtraction. $A ackslash B$ (read “$A$ set-minus $B$”) denotes the set that contains all the elements in $A$ except any that are also in $B$. Formally, $A ackslash B = \{s \in A : s 
otin B\}$. $A ackslash B$ is called the relative complement of $B$ in $A$, since $A ackslash B = A \cup B^C$. [Corrected statement] ... $A ackslash B$ is called the relative complement of $B$ in $A$, since $A ackslash B = A \cap B^C$ (the complement being taken relative to the universal set $U$). [Formal content] Let $U$ be a set and $A, B \subseteq U$, with $B^C = \{s \in U : s 
otin B\}$. Then $A ackslash B = \{s \in A : s 
otin B\} = A \cap B^C$. The printed identity $A ackslash B = A \cup B^C$ holds if and only if $A \cup B = U$ and $A \cap B = \emptyset$, that is, if and only if $A = B^C$; for example, with $U = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $A = \{1, 2\}$ and $B = \{2\}$: $A ackslash B = \{1\}$, $A \cap B^C = \{1\}$ and $A \cup B^C = \{1, 2, 3\}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Glossary of Mathematical Notation, p. 283] The complement of a set. When all sets under consideration are subsets of some universal set $U$, the complement of a set $A$ is the set of all elements in $U$ that are not in $A$. Formally, $A^C = \{s \in U : s \notin A\}$. The union of sets: $A \cup B = \{s : s \in A \text{ or } s \in B\}$. The intersection of sets: $A \cap B = \{s : s \in A \text{ and } s \in B\}$. Subset: $A \subseteq B \iff \forall s \in A$, $s \in B$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): a union is printed where an intersection is required; the row's own definition $\{s \in A : s \notin B\}$ is correct. canonical_claim.statement: [p. 166] Let us assume that the CEF is differentiable with respect to a given variable $X_{[k]}$.$^{13}$ Then, the partial derivative of the CEF with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $\left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}}$. [Footnote 13] Beyond requiring that the CEF be differentiable at every value of $\mathbf{X}$ with positive support, this characterization only makes sense when $\mathbf{X}$ is continuous. When $\mathbf{X}$ is discrete, we would recommend computing variants of discrete analogs to partial derivatives, such as partial slopes. [p. 167] The partial derivative at the average represents a conceptually different target: how much a change in a particular variable $X_{[k]}$ moves the CEF when all variables in $\mathbf{X}$ are equal to their expected value. It is the slope of the CEF with respect to $X_{[k]}$ at a single point. Definition 4.3.7. Partial Derivative at the Average. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$, the partial derivative at the average of the CEF (of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$) with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]}$. Again, a natural plug-in estimator is available for $PDA_{X_{[k]}}$, which replaces the expected values with sample means, and the CEF with the estimated CEF. The plug-in estimate of the partial derivative at the average with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $\widehat{PDA}_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \overline{\mathbf{X}}}$. [p. 168] While the partial derivative at the average also has a well-defined meaning, it is limited to just one particular point on the probability distribution of the explanatory variables.

canonical_claim.statement: [pp. 198–199] Suppose that the distribution of $Y$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as a weighted average of $M$ different parametric models, $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_1g_1(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_1) + p_2g_2(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_2) + ... + \left(1 - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} p_m\right)g_M(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_M)$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_1, \boldsymbol\theta_1, p_2, \boldsymbol\theta_2, ..., p_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_M)$. Then, as before, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ can be maximized to find the ML estimate of $\boldsymbol\theta$. (This can sometimes be computationally tricky.) If any subset of the models in $(g_1(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_1), ..., g_M(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_M))$ jointly characterize the conditional distribution of $Y$, then this estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient. When the models are not valid (even jointly), our estimates should be interpreted explicitly as an approximation. [Example 5.2.11, p. 200] Consider a mixture model that incorporates all three models: $g(y; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_Ng_N(y; (\mu_N, \sigma_N)) + p_{LN}g_{LN}(y; (\mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN})) + (1 - p_N - p_{LN})g_E(y; \lambda_E) = p_N\frac{1}{\sigma_N\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(y - \mu_N)^2}{2\sigma_N^2}} + p_{LN}\frac{1}{y\sigma_{LN}\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(\log y - \mu_{LN})^2}{2\sigma_{LN}^2}} + (1 - p_N - p_{LN})\lambda_Ee^{-\lambda_Ey}$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_N, p_{LN}, \mu_N, \sigma_N, \mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E)$. Figure 5.2.5 visualizes the ML estimate of this mixture model, which provides a markedly better approximation. [The two printed claims, as statements] (A) For every sample, the likelihood $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ of a mixture model has a maximizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$. (B) If the conditional distribution of $Y$ is a mixture of a subset of the component models, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ is asymptotically efficient.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood.
canonical_claim.note: The passage as printed, for the two Moderate findings on it: claim (A) is P001-C05-E002 (it fails for the example's own unrestricted mixture; counterexample target), and claim (B) is P001-C05-N005 (it fails for the displayed full parameter vector when a component is unused; counterexample target). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.3, the claims relating positivity and overlap around Definition 7.3.1 and Theorem 7.3.2, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 271 (PDF p. 289); p. 272 (PDF p. 290), with Example 7.3.3
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 271] In practice, even if the positivity assumption holds, but $\exists\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$ such that $p_D(\mathbf{x})$ is near zero or one, then difficulties in estimation may ensue. Both of these issues are tied to the idea of “overlap” in the distributions of $\mathbf{X}_i$ across treatment and control arms. We proceed by illustrating that a failure of the positivity assumption logically implies incomplete (or “limited”) overlap in the population of interest. When the positivity assumption fails, then the distributions of $\mathbf{X}_i$ for treated and control units have regions with positive probability that do not completely overlap with one another. This notion of overlap is formalized in the following definition. Definition 7.3.1. Complete Population Overlap. Let $D_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then $D_i$ has complete population overlap with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 1] = \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 0]$. Overlap simply implies that, if there exists a covariate value in the treatment group with positive (conditional) density, then that covariate value also has positive density conditional on being the control group, and vice versa. We now state our primary result in this section, which establishes that positivity and overlap are tightly connected. Theorem 7.3.2. Positivity Implies Complete Population Overlap. Let $D_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. If $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$, then $D_i$ has complete population overlap with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$. Furthermore, the converse of this claim (that population overlap implies positivity) can almost be stated here, but requires some measure-theoretic conditions on support. We omit the formal proof, but provide an illustrative example in the case of a single covariate. [Example 7.3.3, p. 272] ... Note that the failures of overlap and positivity occur in exactly the same regions: in the upper range of $X_i$, where there are treated units but no control units, the propensity score must equal one, and in the ranges where there are control units but no treated units, the propensity score must equal zero. [The three printed claims, as statements] (A) Theorem 7.3.2. (B) If there is no $\epsilon > 0$ with $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$, then $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 1] \ne \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 0]$. (C) If $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 1] = \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 0]$, then (under unspecified conditions on support) there is $\epsilon > 0$ with $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] Treatment Propensity Function. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$. Then the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is also known as the propensity score for unit $i$.
canonical_claim.note: The passage as printed, for the Moderate finding P001-C07-E008. (A) is true; (B) is the contrapositive of (C) without its hedge, and both fail for the countable example of the counterexample target. Example 7.3.3 and Figure 7.3.1 illustrate only propensity scores equal to zero or one on part of the support, for which the description is correct.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.5, the paragraph justifying ignorability in the application, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: The fact that random assignment is unlikely to hold does not mean that all hope is lost. This is a setting where the ignorability assumption, implying $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$, is quite plausible. As long as voters do not directly know the applicant, the applicant description contains all of the information available to voters. Assuming that the researchers' coding of the applicant descriptions—that is, the variables in $\mathbf{X}_i$—does indeed account for all the information presented to the voters, then, by definition, $D_i$ must be conditionally independent of potential outcomes. [The printed implication, as a statement] Let the units be referenda with potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$ (the 'no' vote share with the applicant identified as female or as male, the description otherwise exactly as it was), treatment $D_i$ and covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$. If $(\mathbf{X}_i, D_i)$ records all the information about the applicant that is presented to the voters of referendum $i$, and the voters have no other information about the applicant, then $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] Strong Ignorability. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$. Then $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if the following conditions hold: $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ (conditional independence assumption); $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$ (positivity).
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, for the Moderate finding P001-C07-E010. It is an interpretive claim about an application; the last paragraph is the formal implication that 'by definition' asserts, which the four-atom counterexample refutes. 'All the information presented to the voters' has no formal definition in the book; the validators model it by letting each electorate's votes depend only on the leaflet content $(\mathbf{X}_i, D_i)$ and on the electorate's own preferences.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 2.1.9 (Linearity of Expectations), Theorem 2.1.13 (Alternative Formula for Variance), Theorem 2.1.14 (Properties of Variance), Theorem 2.1.16 (Properties of Standard Deviation) and Theorem 2.1.18 (Chebyshev's Inequality)

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 2.1.9. Linearity of Expectations. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then, $\forall a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{E}[aX + bY + c] = a\mathrm{E}[X] + b\mathrm{E}[Y] + c$. Theorem 2.1.13. Alternative Formula for Variance. For a random variable $X$, $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \mathrm{E}[X]^2$. Theorem 2.1.14. Properties of Variance. For a random variable $X$, $\forall c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{V}[X + c] = \mathrm{V}[X]$; $\forall a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{V}[aX] = a^2\mathrm{V}[X]$. Theorem 2.1.16. Properties of Standard Deviation. For a random variable $X$, $\forall c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma[X + c] = \sigma[X]$; $\forall a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma[aX] = |a|\sigma[X]$. Theorem 2.1.18. Chebyshev's Inequality. Let $X$ be a random variable with finite $\sigma[X] > 0$. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, $\Pr\left[|X - \mathrm{E}[X]| \ge \epsilon\sigma[X]\right] \le \frac{1}{\epsilon^2}$.

[Footnote 3, p. 49] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [both discrete with joint PMF, or jointly continuous with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Footnote 7, p. 55] Moments, including the expected value, can be infinite or undefined; this is why we invoked the condition of absolute convergence in Definition 2.1.1.

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 3.2.3. The Expected Value of the Sample Mean Is the Population Mean. For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mathrm{E}[X]$. Theorem 3.2.4. Sampling Variance of the Sample Mean. For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X]$, the sampling variance of $\overline{X}$ is $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\mathrm{V}[X]}{n}$. Theorem 3.2.5. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 4.3.3 (Polynomial Approximation of the CEF), with Theorem 4.3.2 (Weierstrass Approximation Theorem)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 4.3.2. Weierstrass Approximation Theorem. Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, there exists a polynomial $p$ such that $\forall x \in [a, b]$, $|f(x) - p(x)| < \epsilon$. Theorem 4.3.3. Polynomial Approximation of the CEF. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables, and suppose that $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$ is continuous and $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = [a, b]$. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, $\exists K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that, $\forall K' \ge K$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\mathrm{E}[Y|X] - g(X, X^2, ..., X^{K'})\right)^2\right] < \epsilon$, where $g(X, X^2, ..., X^{K'})$ is the BLP of $Y$ given $X, X^2, ..., X^{K'}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 2.3.6, p. 86 (PDF p. 104)] the BLP of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X} = (X_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]})$ is $g(\mathbf{X}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{[1]} + ... + \beta_KX_{[K]}$ with $(\beta_0, ..., \beta_K)$ minimizing $\mathrm{E}[(Y - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]} + ... + b_KX_{[K]}))^2]$; here $X_{[k]} = X^k$. [p. 86] The BLP is also the best linear approximation of the CEF; setting $(b_0, ..., b_K) = (\beta_0, ..., \beta_K)$ minimizes $\mathrm{E}[(\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}] - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]} + ... + b_KX_{[K]}))^2]$.

The printed proof: by Theorem 4.3.2 there is a polynomial $p$ with $|\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] - p(x)| < \sqrt{\epsilon}$ on $[a, b]$, so $\mathrm{E}[(\mathrm{E}[Y|X] - p(X))^2] < \epsilon$; with $K = \deg p$, the BLP on $X, ..., X^{K'}$ is the minimum-MSE predictor of $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ among polynomials of degree at most $K'$, so its error is no larger for every $K' \ge K$. The book omits the proof of Theorem 4.3.2. Finite second moments are implicit, and for large $K'$ the BLP coefficients need not be unique although the BLP as a function on the support is.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 5.2.3 (Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Biased Coin Flip): the ML estimate of $p$ is the sample mean
canonical_claim.statement: [Setting, p. 187] As usual, let $Y = 0$ if the coin comes up heads and $Y = 1$ if the coin comes up tails. Our model is $f_Y(y) = g(y; p) = 1 - p$ for $y = 0$, $p$ for $y = 1$, and $0$ otherwise, with $\boldsymbol\Theta = [0, 1]$. Suppose that we observed $n$ i.i.d. coin flips: $\mathbf{Y} = (Y_1, Y_2, ..., Y_n)^T$. [The three cases, p. 188] First, suppose that $\mathbf{Y} = (0, 0, ..., 0)^T$. Then $\mathcal{L}(\hat p|\mathbf{Y}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - \hat p) = (1 - \hat p)^n$, which, among all $\hat p \in [0, 1]$, is clearly maximized at $\hat p = 0 = \overline{Y}$. Now, suppose that $\mathbf{Y} = (1, 1, ..., 1)^T$. Then $\mathcal{L}(\hat p|\mathbf{Y}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\hat p = \hat p^n$, which, among all $\hat p \in [0, 1]$, is clearly maximized at $\hat p = 1 = \overline{Y}$. Finally, suppose that $\exists i$ such that $Y_i = 0$ and $\exists i'$ such that $Y_{i'} = 1$. Let $I_0 = \{i : Y_i = 0\}$ and $I_1 = \{i : Y_i = 1\}$. Then $\mathcal{L}(\hat p|\mathbf{Y}) = \prod_{i \in I_0}(1 - \hat p)\prod_{i \in I_1}\hat p = (1 - \hat p)^{N_0}\hat p^{N_1}$, where $N_0 = |I_0|$ and $N_1 = |I_1|$; $\log\mathcal{L}(\hat p|\mathbf{Y}) = N_0\log(1 - \hat p) + N_1\log(\hat p)$; the first-order condition $-\frac{N_0}{1 - \hat p} + \frac{N_1}{\hat p} = 0$ gives [p. 189] $\hat p = \frac{N_1}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i = \overline{Y}$. [Conclusion, p. 189] Thus, the ML estimate of the probability of the coin coming up tails is the proportion of flips that came up tails—in other words, the sample mean. ... suppose that we tossed the coin $n = 3$ times and observed $\mathbf{Y} = (1, 0, 1)$. ... The ML estimate for $p$ corresponds to the maximum in the figure: $\hat p_{ML} = \frac{2}{3}$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 6.1.6 (Expected Value under MCAR), Theorem 6.1.9 (Expected Value under MAR) and Theorem 6.1.10 (CEF under MAR); with the estimates of Examples 6.1.7 and 6.2.1
canonical_claim.location: Definition 6.1.5 and Theorem 6.1.6: p. 213 (PDF p. 231). Example 6.1.7: p. 214 (PDF p. 232). Definition 6.1.8: p. 215 (PDF p. 233). Theorem 6.1.9: p. 216 (PDF p. 234). Theorem 6.1.10: p. 217 (PDF p. 235). Section 6.2.1 and Example 6.2.1: pp. 219–220 (PDF pp. 237–238)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 6.1.6. Expected Value under MCAR. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$. Then, if $Y_i$ is missing completely at random, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]$. Theorem 6.1.9. Expected Value under MAR. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a discrete random vector. [Footnote 8: We assume here that $\mathbf{X}_i$ is discrete for ease of exposition. ... Recall that we are writing $\sum_{\mathbf{x}}$ as a shorthand for $\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]}$.] Then, if $Y_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]\Pr[\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$. Theorem 6.1.10. CEF under MAR. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, if $Y_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i]$. [Plug-in estimators and the worked numbers] [p. 214] Under MCAR, $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i] = \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1] = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i^*R_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i}$; in Example 6.1.2 (units $1, ..., 6$ with $Y_i^* = 1, -99, 1, 0, 1, -99$ and $R_i = 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0$) the estimate is $\frac{3}{4}$. [p. 219] Under MAR with discrete covariates, $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i] = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i^*R_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{n}$, where $\widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]$ is the set of all observed values of $\mathbf{X}_i$. [Example 6.2.1, p. 220] With the binary covariate $X_i = 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1$ for units $1, ..., 6$: $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i] = \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, X_i = 0]\widehat{\Pr}[X_i = 0] + \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, X_i = 1]\widehat{\Pr}[X_i = 1] = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{6} + 1 \cdot \frac{2}{6} = \frac{7}{9}$.

For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213] Missing Completely at Random (MCAR). Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$. Then $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if the following conditions hold: $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ (independence of outcome and response); $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$ (nonzero probability of response). [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] Missing at Random (MAR). Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. [Footnote 6] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. If $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$, all the implications of independence derived in Chapters 1 and 2 hold conditional on $X$; for example, $\mathrm{E}[Y|X] = \mathrm{E}[Y|Z, X]$. [Footnote 7] The statement that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$ is equivalent to $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 10, p. 219] The plug-in estimator requires that we have at least one unit who responded with $\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}$ for every covariate profile $\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]$.

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 6.1.12. MAR and the Propensity Score. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, if $Y_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, - $R_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathbf{X}_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$. (Balance conditional on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$) - $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$. (Independence of outcome and response conditional on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$) - $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] > \epsilon$. (Nonzero probability of response conditional on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$) [Proof, p. 218: 'We will prove the first two properties and omit a proof of the third.'] Balance: since $R_i$ is binary, $R_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \mathbf{X}_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) \iff \mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i, p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] = \mathrm{E}[R_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)]$; $\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i, p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] = \mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$, and by the Law of Iterated Expectations $\mathrm{E}[R_i|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] = \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i]|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] = \mathrm{E}[p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)|p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)] = p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$. canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 6.2.9. Double Robustness Theorem for Missing Data. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Let $\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$ be an approximation of the CEF evaluated at $R_i = 1$ and $\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}$, and let $\tilde p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ be an approximation of the propensity score. If MAR holds and if either (i) $\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \tilde p_R(\mathbf{x}) < 1 - \epsilon$, or (ii) $\tilde p_R(\mathbf{x}) = p_R(\mathbf{x})$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, then $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i] + \frac{R_i\left(Y_i^* - \tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i]\right)}{\tilde p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 7.1.7 (Sharp Bounds for the ATE) and the width of the bounds; with the estimates of Example 7.1.6
canonical_claim.location: Theorem 7.1.7: p. 241 (PDF p. 259); proof on pp. 241–242 (PDF pp. 259–260). Width: pp. 242–243 (PDF pp. 260–261). Example 7.1.6: p. 240 (PDF p. 258)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 7.1.7. Sharp Bounds for the ATE. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables such that, $\forall d \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i(d)] \subseteq [a, b]$, and $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. Then $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i] \in \Big[\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1]\Pr[D_i = 1] + a\Pr[D_i = 0] - \left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0]\Pr[D_i = 0] + b\Pr[D_i = 1]\right),\ \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1]\Pr[D_i = 1] + b\Pr[D_i = 0] - \left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0]\Pr[D_i = 0] + a\Pr[D_i = 1]\right)\Big]$. [p. 242] One interesting feature of these bounds is that their width is always $(b - a)$, and does not depend on any other feature of the data. [Example 7.1.6, p. 240] With binary outcomes ($a = 0$, $b = 1$) and the six units of Example 7.1.5 (units $1, ..., 6$ with $D_i = 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0$ and observed outcomes $Y_i = 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0$): plugging in one for the missing values of $Y_i(1)$ and zero for the missing values of $Y_i(0)$, the estimate of an upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$ is $\frac{5}{6}$ and of a lower bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)]$ is $\frac{1}{6}$, so the estimate of an upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6}$; the estimated lower bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$ is $\frac{3}{6}$ and the estimated upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)]$ is $\frac{5}{6}$, so the estimated lower bound for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\frac{3}{6} - \frac{5}{6} = -\frac{2}{6}$. [Sharpness, as asserted in the prose, p. 244: 'Without adding assumptions, these bounds are tight'] For every value $c$ in the interval there are random variables $(Y_i'(0), Y_i'(1), D_i')$ with supports in $[a, b]$ and $\{0, 1\}$ whose observable pair $(Y_i', D_i')$ has the same joint distribution as $(Y_i, D_i)$ and for which $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i'] = c$.

[Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$.
